def: Buildup of thickened, degenerated elastic fibers in the dermis, usually from chronic sun exposure (solar elastosis), giving leathery, wrinkled, yellowed skin. It is a hallmark finding beneath actinic keratosis.
Oval or cigar-shaped red blood cells seen on a smear. They are typical of hereditary elliptocytosis, caused by defective spectrin or other red cell membrane skeleton proteins.
An HIV drug that blocks integrase, the viral enzyme that inserts viral DNA into the host genome. It is boosted with cobicistat and used in combination pills.
The inner cell mass of the blastocyst, the cluster of cells that goes on to form the embryo itself. The outer trophoblast forms the placenta.
A moisturizing agent applied to skin to soften it and trap water, used in dry skin conditions such as atopic dermatitis.

Another name for Sturge-Weber syndrome, a sporadic disorder with a facial port-wine stain along the trigeminal nerve distribution, leptomeningeal vascular malformations, seizures and glaucoma. It results from a somatic GNAQ mutation.
Describing a reaction with positive change in free energy (positive delta G) that needs energy input to proceed. Cells drive these by coupling them to ATP hydrolysis.
A fabric-covered stent placed inside a blood vessel to line it and exclude an aneurysm from circulation. It is used in endovascular aneurysm repair of the aorta.
The inner part of the heart wall, consisting of the endocardial lining and the adjacent muscle layer. Endomyocardial biopsy samples it to diagnose myocarditis, amyloidosis and transplant rejection.
Relating to the endoneurium, the delicate connective tissue that surrounds each individual nerve fiber (axon) inside a nerve fascicle.
An injectable HIV fusion inhibitor that binds the viral gp41 protein and prevents the virus from fusing with the host cell membrane.
A drug that blocks catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT), slowing levodopa breakdown. It is added to levodopa-carbidopa in Parkinson disease to reduce wearing-off.
A nucleoside analog that inhibits hepatitis B virus DNA polymerase, used to treat chronic hepatitis B.
Describing a strain of Escherichia coli (EAEC) that adheres to intestinal cells in a stacked-brick pattern and causes persistent watery diarrhea, especially in children and travelers.
A herniation of small bowel into the vaginal wall, usually through a weakened pelvic floor, forming a type of pelvic organ prolapse.
Describing the neuroendocrine cells of the gut lining that make serotonin. Tumors from these cells are carcinoid tumors.
Imaging of the small bowel with CT or MRI after the patient drinks a large volume of contrast. It is used to evaluate Crohn disease and bowel bleeding.
Connecting the bowel and the bladder, as in an enterovesical fistula. Diverticulitis and Crohn disease are common causes, and it presents with pneumaturia and fecaluria.
Brand name of a combination of sacubitril, a neprilysin inhibitor, and valsartan, an angiotensin receptor blocker. It is used in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.
To remove an organ or mass whole from its surrounding tissue, or to surgically remove the eyeball. Also describes a cell that has lost its nucleus.
An abnormally low eosinophil count in the blood, seen with acute stress and with glucocorticoid excess such as Cushing syndrome.
Eosinophils in the urine, classically associated with acute interstitial nephritis caused by drugs such as penicillins and NSAIDs.
Small flat tan to brown spots on sun-exposed skin, common in fair-skinned people. They darken with sunlight and have a normal number of melanocytes with increased melanin.
The upper central region of the abdomen, just below the sternum and above the umbilicus. Pain here is typical of peptic ulcer disease and pancreatitis.
Describing EEG patterns, such as spikes and sharp waves, that resemble those seen in epilepsy.
Relating to the omentum. Epiploic appendages are small fat-filled pouches along the surface of the colon, and the epiploic foramen links the lesser and greater sacs of the peritoneum.
A chemotherapy drug that inhibits microtubule growth, used in metastatic breast cancer.
An antisense oligonucleotide that causes exon 51 skipping so a shortened but functional dystrophin is made, used for certain Duchenne muscular dystrophy mutations.
A second-generation non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor used for HIV that has become resistant to earlier drugs in its class.

Describing the tall, long-limbed body proportions seen when sex hormones are deficient before puberty, because the growth plates close late. Arm span exceeds height, as in Klinefelter syndrome and Kallmann syndrome.
Describing a widespread skin rash, such as the rashes of measles, rubella and drug reactions.
Describing a reaction with negative change in free energy (negative delta G) that releases energy and can proceed spontaneously, such as ATP hydrolysis.
The outer part of the uterine cervix that projects into the vagina, covered by stratified squamous epithelium. It meets the columnar epithelium of the endocervix at the transformation zone.
Bulging of the eyes caused by swelling of the tissue behind them. It is typical of the eye disease of Graves disease.
A nuclear receptor in liver and gut activated by bile acids. It lowers bile acid synthesis and uptake, and is targeted by obeticholic acid in primary biliary cholangitis.
A bundle of fibers wrapped in connective tissue, such as a bundle of muscle fibers (perimysium) or of nerve axons (perineurium).
The probability of achieving pregnancy in a single menstrual cycle in a couple having unprotected intercourse.
Small pores in the endothelial lining of capillaries that permit rapid exchange of fluid and small molecules, found in the kidney glomerulus, intestines and endocrine glands.
Small openings or pores in a membrane or vessel wall, such as the pores in glomerular and hepatic sinusoidal endothelium.
A second-generation H1 antihistamine used for allergic rhinitis and hives. It causes little sedation because it barely crosses the blood-brain barrier.

A group of benign but locally aggressive tumors of fibroblasts that infiltrate surrounding tissue and recur after removal but do not metastasize. Desmoid tumors in familial adenomatous polyposis are an example.
